subtopics.title: Meaning and Scope of Biology
subtopics.content:
Biology is the scientific study of life and living organisms. The word comes from
Greek roots: bios, meaning life, and logos/logy, meaning study. Biology examines
the structure, organisation, functions, growth, reproduction, inheritance,
evolution, interactions and distribution of living organisms.

Biology is both a theoretical and practical science. Learners observe organisms,
collect evidence, formulate questions, test ideas, record observations, analyse
data and draw conclusions. Biological knowledge is applied to medicine,
agriculture, food production, conservation, biotechnology, public health and
environmental management.

A living organism is recognised by a combination of characteristics of life:
nutrition, respiration, excretion, growth, sensitivity/response, movement,
reproduction and cellular organisation. These characteristics should be
considered together rather than using only one feature to decide whether
something is living.

Levels of biological organisation can be viewed from cell -> tissue -> organ ->
organ system -> organism -> population -> community -> ecosystem -> biosphere.
A cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life. A tissue is a group
of similar cells performing a particular function. An organ contains different
tissues working together. An organ system contains organs that cooperate to
perform major functions.

Biology in Zimbabwe is important for food security, human health, conservation
of biodiversity, livestock production, crop improvement, water management,
disease control and sustainable use of natural resources.

DETAILED STUDY AND EXAMINATION NOTES

Core terminology:
Learners should be able to define the important terms in this subtopic accurately,
use them in biological context, and distinguish closely related terms. In an
examination, definitions should identify the process, the direction or relationship
involved, and any condition that makes the definition precise.

Understanding relationships:
Biology questions often test relationships rather than isolated facts. When explaining
a process, state the starting condition, describe what changes, identify the mechanism
responsible, and state the result. Where a structure is described, link each important
feature to its function. Where a factor affects a process, state the direction of the
effect and explain the biological reason.

Application:
The knowledge in Meaning and Scope of Biology should be applied to unfamiliar examples, diagrams, tables,
graphs and everyday situations. Students should practise identifying variables,
predicting outcomes, explaining observations and drawing conclusions supported by
evidence. Zimbabwean examples should be interpreted scientifically: local crops,
livestock, wildlife, water resources, public-health programmes and environmental
conditions can provide useful contexts for applying the same biological principles.

Practical skills:
For investigations related to this subtopic, identify the independent variable,
dependent variable and controlled variables. Use an appropriate control where
possible. Keep quantities and procedures consistent, repeat measurements, calculate
averages where appropriate, identify anomalous results, present results in a suitable
table or graph and draw a conclusion that directly answers the investigation question.
Safety precautions must be specific to the actual hazard rather than simply stating
"be careful".

Exam technique:
For a "state" question, give the required fact without unnecessary explanation. For
"describe", give observable features or sequential events. For "explain", give the
reason or mechanism. For "compare", provide paired similarities or differences using
the same basis of comparison. For "suggest", apply known biological principles to the
new situation and make the reasoning explicit. For calculations, show working,
include units and check whether the final value is biologically sensible.

Common errors to avoid:
Do not confuse structure with function, diffusion with osmosis, active transport with
passive transport, genotype with phenotype, or respiration with breathing. Do not use
arrows ambiguously in food chains. Do not claim that every change in phenotype is
caused by a change in DNA. Do not describe a correlation as proof of causation without
evidence. Use correct biological vocabulary and avoid everyday meanings where they
conflict with scientific meanings.

main mechanism, label or interpret relevant biological structures, compare related
concepts, describe a suitable practical investigation, interpret simple experimental
data, and apply the topic to a new biological situation.

subtopics.title: Branches of Biology
subtopics.content:
Cytology is the study of cells and their structure and functions.
Anatomy is the study of the internal and external structure of organisms.
Physiology is the study of how organs and body systems function.
Ecology is the study of relationships between organisms and their environment.
Genetics is the study of heredity, genes, chromosomes and variation.
Microbiology is the study of microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi and some
microscopic protists.
Zoology is the study of animals.
Botany is the study of plants.
Biotechnology applies organisms, cells or biological molecules to produce useful
products and processes.
Systematics/taxonomy deals with identification, naming and classification of
organisms.
Conservation biology focuses on protection and sustainable management of
biodiversity and ecosystems.

subtopics.title: Biology-Related Careers
subtopics.content:
Biology provides a foundation for careers including medical doctor, nurse,
laboratory scientist, biomedical scientist, pharmacist, veterinarian, dietician,
ecologist, conservationist, wildlife officer, agricultural scientist, crop
scientist, microbiologist, geneticist, biotechnology specialist, environmental
scientist, fisheries officer, science teacher, research scientist and food
technologist.

A biology-related career normally requires scientific knowledge, careful
observation, communication, data handling, ethical behaviour and practical
skills. Careers should be linked to national needs such as disease prevention,
food production, environmental protection and sustainable development.

subtopics.title: Laboratory Safety and Emergency Procedures
subtopics.content:
Common causes of laboratory accidents include fire, fumes, acids and strong
bases, microorganisms, improper handling of apparatus and electricity.

General rules include wearing appropriate protective equipment; tying back long
hair; keeping benches clean and dry; never tasting laboratory chemicals; not
eating or drinking in the laboratory; reading labels before use; using apparatus
correctly; reporting breakages and injuries immediately; washing hands after
practical work; and disposing of biological and chemical waste safely.

Goggles protect the eyes from splashes and particles. Gloves reduce contact with
hazardous substances and biological material. A fume cupboard reduces exposure
to harmful fumes. A fire extinguisher is used only when the user has been
trained and the situation is appropriate. A fire blanket can smother suitable
fires. A sand bucket may be used for certain small fires.

During an emergency, alert the teacher or responsible adult, raise the alarm,
remove people from danger, use the appropriate emergency procedure and seek
first aid. Fire drills should be treated seriously. Electrical equipment should
not be handled with wet hands. Damaged electrical leads must not be used.

For biological materials, avoid direct contact, use suitable containment and
disinfect or dispose of materials according to laboratory instructions. Sharp
objects must be handled carefully and disposed of in suitable containers.

subtopics.title: Safety Labels and Hazard Symbols
subtopics.content:
Hazard labels communicate risks before a substance or piece of equipment is
handled. Learners should be able to recognise common symbols for flammable,
corrosive, toxic, harmful/irritant, explosive, oxidising and biohazardous
materials where applicable.

A flammable warning indicates that a substance can catch fire easily. A
corrosive warning indicates that a substance can damage tissue or corrode
materials. A toxic warning indicates a serious poisoning hazard. An irritant
warning indicates that exposure can cause irritation or harm. An oxidising
warning indicates that a substance can intensify combustion. A biohazard
warning indicates biological material that may present a health hazard.

The safe response is not merely to memorise the symbol: identify the hazard,
assess the risk, use the correct protective equipment, follow instructions and
dispose of waste safely.

subtopics.title: Water: Structure and Properties
subtopics.content:
Water is composed of hydrogen and oxygen, with the molecular formula H2O.
The molecule has a bent structure and is polar because oxygen attracts the shared
electrons more strongly than hydrogen. Hydrogen bonds form between neighbouring
water molecules.

Water is an excellent solvent for many ionic and polar substances. This makes it
useful in cytoplasm, blood, tissue fluid and plant sap and allows dissolved
substances to be transported. It participates in metabolic reactions and is a
reactant in hydrolysis and photosynthesis.

Water has a relatively high specific heat capacity, so large amounts of heat are
required to change its temperature. This helps organisms and aquatic habitats
resist rapid temperature changes. Water also has a high latent heat of
vaporisation, making evaporation an effective cooling process in sweating and
transpiration.

Cohesion between water molecules helps maintain continuous water columns in
xylem. Adhesion helps water interact with vessel walls. Ice is less dense than
liquid water because hydrogen bonding produces a more open structure when water
freezes; therefore ice floats and can form an insulating surface on ponds.

Water is essential as a habitat because aquatic organisms depend on its physical
properties, dissolved oxygen, dissolved nutrients and temperature stability.

subtopics.title: Carbohydrates: Classes and Uses
subtopics.content:
Carbohydrates contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Monosaccharides are single
sugar units, for example glucose. Disaccharides contain two monosaccharide units,
for example sucrose. Polysaccharides contain many sugar units, for example
starch, glycogen and cellulose.

Glucose is an important respiratory substrate and is transported in blood.
Sucrose is the main transport sugar in many flowering plants. Starch is a storage
polysaccharide in plants; it is compact and insoluble enough to be stored without
greatly lowering cell water potential. Glycogen is a storage carbohydrate in
animals and fungi. Cellulose forms much of the plant cell wall and gives cells
mechanical strength.

The arrangement of glucose units determines the properties of polysaccharides.
Starch and glycogen are suited to storage, while cellulose forms strong fibres.

subtopics.title: Proteins and Amino Acids
subtopics.content:
Proteins are nitrogen-containing biological molecules made from amino acids.
An amino acid contains an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and a
variable R group attached to a central carbon atom.

Amino acids join by peptide bonds to form polypeptide chains. A protein may
consist of one or more folded polypeptide chains. The sequence of amino acids
determines the final three-dimensional structure and therefore the function.

Protein functions include forming structural materials such as collagen and
keratin; acting as enzymes; transporting substances such as oxygen by
haemoglobin; forming antibodies; contributing to hormones such as insulin;
forming contractile structures in muscles; and participating in blood clotting.

Heat and extreme pH can denature many proteins by disrupting bonds maintaining
their shape. Denaturation can permanently change enzyme active sites.

subtopics.title: Fats and Lipids
subtopics.content:
Lipids include fats and oils. Many fats are formed from glycerol and fatty acids.
They are largely insoluble in water.

Lipids provide concentrated energy reserves, form part of cell membranes as
phospholipids, provide thermal insulation, cushion and protect organs, and
contribute to waterproofing. Plants commonly store oils in seeds, while animals
may store fat in adipose tissue.

Because lipids contain many carbon-hydrogen bonds, oxidation releases substantial
energy. Stored fat can therefore provide a long-term energy reserve.

subtopics.title: Nucleic Acids
subtopics.content:
DNA and RNA are nucleic acids. Their basic building blocks are nucleotides.
A nucleotide contains a sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogen-containing base.

DNA stores hereditary information. The sequence of bases forms a code used in
directing the production of proteins. RNA has important roles in using genetic
information during protein synthesis.

DNA is normally double stranded, with complementary base pairing. Adenine pairs
with thymine and cytosine pairs with guanine in DNA. RNA commonly contains

subtopics.title: Food Tests and Interpretation
subtopics.content:
Benedict's test is used for reducing sugars. A sample is mixed with Benedict's
solution and heated. A negative result remains blue; increasing amounts of
reducing sugar produce a change through green/yellow/orange to a brick-red
precipitate. The test is therefore qualitative unless a standardised quantitative
method is used.

Non-reducing sugars such as sucrose can be tested by first hydrolysing them with
dilute acid, neutralising the mixture and then carrying out Benedict's test.

Iodine solution tests for starch. A positive result is blue-black; a negative
result remains yellow-brown.

Biuret reagent tests for protein. A positive result is lilac/purple; a negative
result remains blue.

The emulsion test is used for lipids. The food sample is mixed with ethanol and
then water. A positive result is a cloudy white emulsion.

Practical accuracy requires clean apparatus, suitable controls, consistent
sample volumes and careful observation of colour changes.

subtopics.title: Plant and Animal Cell Structure
subtopics.content:
The cell is the basic unit of living organisms. Plant and animal cells contain
cell surface membranes, cytoplasm, nuclei and mitochondria, although the
structures and proportions vary.

The cell surface membrane forms a selectively permeable boundary controlling
movement of substances into and out of the cell. Cytoplasm is the site of many
metabolic reactions. The nucleus contains chromosomes and controls cellular
activities through gene expression.

Mitochondria are sites of aerobic respiration and ATP production. Ribosomes are
involved in protein synthesis.

Plant cells additionally have a cellulose cell wall, a large permanent vacuole
containing cell sap and chloroplasts in photosynthetic tissues. Chloroplasts
contain chlorophyll and are the main sites of photosynthesis.

A good biological drawing should show clear continuous lines, no unnecessary
shading, correct proportions, labels placed neatly and a descriptive title.

subtopics.title: Cell Specialisation
subtopics.content:
Cells become specialised when they develop structures suited to particular
functions.

A red blood cell has a biconcave shape giving a large surface area, contains
haemoglobin and lacks a nucleus when mature, allowing more room for oxygen
transport.

A sperm cell has a flagellum for movement, many mitochondria to supply energy
and an acrosome containing enzymes used during fertilisation.

A ciliated epithelial cell has cilia that move mucus and trapped particles.
A root hair cell has a long extension increasing surface area for water and
mineral uptake.

A palisade cell contains many chloroplasts and is positioned near the upper
surface of the leaf to maximise light absorption. Xylem vessels are hollow,
strengthened by lignin and adapted for water transport and support. Muscle cells
contain contractile proteins and many mitochondria for movement.

subtopics.title: Diffusion
subtopics.content:
Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration
to a region of lower concentration as a result of random molecular motion.

Diffusion does not require metabolic energy from the cell. The rate is affected
by the concentration gradient, temperature, surface area and diffusion distance.
Smaller distances and larger surface areas generally increase the rate.

In organisms, oxygen and carbon dioxide move by diffusion across respiratory
surfaces. Carbon dioxide diffuses from respiring cells into blood and then from
blood into alveoli, while oxygen diffuses in the opposite direction at the lungs.

subtopics.title: Osmosis, Turgor and Plasmolysis
subtopics.content:
Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water
potential to a region of lower water potential through a selectively permeable
membrane.

A plant cell in a dilute solution gains water. The vacuole expands and the cell
becomes turgid because the cell wall resists further expansion. Turgor helps
support non-woody plant tissues.

In a concentrated solution, water leaves a plant cell. The vacuole and cytoplasm
shrink and the cell membrane pulls away from the cell wall: this is plasmolysis.
A plasmolysed cell is flaccid and may lose normal function if water loss is severe.

Animal cells do not have a cell wall. In a very dilute solution they may gain
water and burst; in a concentrated solution they lose water and become
crenated/shrunken.

subtopics.title: Active Transport
subtopics.content:
Active transport is the movement of substances against a concentration gradient
using energy released by respiration and specific membrane transport proteins.

Root hair cells use active transport to absorb mineral ions from soil when the
ion concentration in the soil solution is lower than inside the root cells.
Cells lining parts of the kidney also use active transport to selectively
reabsorb useful substances.

Active transport differs from diffusion and osmosis because it requires metabolic
energy and can move substances against the concentration gradient.

subtopics.title: Organisation and Cell Division
subtopics.content:
Cells form tissues, tissues form organs and organs form organ systems. Examples
include muscle tissue, the heart as an organ and the circulatory system as an
organ system.

Before a cell divides, genetic material is copied so that daughter cells receive
genetic information. Cell division is essential for growth, tissue repair and
replacement of worn-out cells. Uncontrolled cell division can result in tumour
formation and cancer.

subtopics.title: Nature and Properties of Enzymes
subtopics.content:
Enzymes are biological catalysts. A catalyst increases the rate of a chemical
reaction without being permanently used up. Most enzymes are proteins.

Enzymes are specific because their three-dimensional active sites have shapes
complementary to particular substrates. The substrate is the reactant on which
an enzyme acts, and the products are formed after the reaction.

Enzymes allow metabolic reactions to occur rapidly at the relatively mild
temperatures and pH values found in living organisms. Examples include
amylase, protease, lipase, catalase and pectinase.

subtopics.title: Lock-and-Key Model and Enzyme Action
subtopics.content:
In the lock-and-key model, the active site has a particular shape that matches
the substrate. The substrate enters the active site to form an enzyme-substrate
complex. The reaction occurs and products leave the active site, leaving the
enzyme available for another substrate molecule.

Enzyme specificity explains why an enzyme that digests starch does not normally
digest proteins. Enzyme activity can be measured by the amount of substrate
used, product formed or time taken for a visible endpoint to occur.

subtopics.title: Temperature and pH
subtopics.content:
Increasing temperature usually increases enzyme activity initially because
molecules move faster and collide more frequently. At an optimum temperature,
activity is greatest. Above the optimum, heat disrupts bonds maintaining the
enzyme's shape and the active site changes; the enzyme becomes denatured.

Each enzyme also has an optimum pH. Moving too far from this pH can alter the
active site and reduce activity. Different enzymes are adapted to different

subtopics.title: Enzyme Applications
subtopics.content:
Enzymes are used in biological washing powders to break down protein, fat and
carbohydrate stains. Proteases help remove protein stains, while lipases help
remove fats.

Pectinase is used in fruit processing to break down pectin and improve juice
extraction and clarification.

Enzymes are also important in food processing, brewing, baking, cheese making
and biotechnology. Industrial enzymes are selected or engineered for suitable
activity, stability and temperature tolerance.

subtopics.title: Plant Nutrition and Photosynthesis
subtopics.content:
Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use light energy to convert
carbon dioxide and water into glucose, releasing oxygen. Chlorophyll absorbs
light energy.

The word equation is:
carbon dioxide + water -> glucose + oxygen
in the presence of light and chlorophyll.

Photosynthesis provides organic food for plants and forms the basis of most food
chains. Glucose can be used in respiration, converted to starch for storage,
used to make cellulose for cell walls, or combined with mineral-derived
compounds to form other substances.

Factors affecting photosynthesis include light intensity, carbon dioxide
concentration and temperature. At low values, increasing a limiting factor can
increase the rate until another factor becomes limiting.

subtopics.title: Leaf Structure and Adaptations
subtopics.content:
A leaf is adapted for photosynthesis. The broad surface provides a large area for
light absorption. The upper epidermis is generally transparent and protects the
leaf. Palisade cells contain many chloroplasts. Spongy mesophyll has air spaces
that facilitate gas diffusion.

Stomata are pores controlled by guard cells. They regulate carbon dioxide entry
and water vapour loss. Veins contain xylem and phloem. Xylem supplies water and
mineral ions; phloem transports assimilates.

A leaf has a balance between efficient photosynthesis and control of water loss.

subtopics.title: Mineral Nutrition
subtopics.content:
Plants require mineral ions in small amounts. Nitrate ions are needed to make
amino acids and proteins and therefore support growth. Magnesium is required
for chlorophyll formation. Phosphate ions are important in ATP, nucleic acids
and membranes. Potassium has roles in enzyme activation and stomatal function.

Deficiency symptoms can help identify mineral shortages. Nitrogen deficiency
commonly causes poor growth and yellowing of older leaves. Magnesium deficiency
can cause chlorosis because magnesium is part of chlorophyll. Phosphate
deficiency can reduce root and shoot development.

Fertilisers can replace nutrients removed from soil, but excessive application
can cause pollution and eutrophication.

subtopics.title: Transpiration and Water Transport
subtopics.content:
Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from plant surfaces, mainly through
stomata. Water evaporates from moist mesophyll surfaces and diffuses out through
stomata down a water vapour concentration gradient.

Transpiration creates a transpiration stream through xylem. Cohesion helps keep
water molecules together, while adhesion helps maintain contact with xylem
walls. Root uptake supplies water to the xylem.

High temperature, moving air and low humidity generally increase transpiration;
high humidity decreases the diffusion gradient and reduces water loss. Plants
reduce water loss using features such as waxy cuticles, sunken stomata, reduced
leaf area and stomatal closure.

subtopics.title: Translocation
subtopics.content:
Translocation is the transport of organic assimilates, especially sucrose, in
phloem from sources to sinks. A source is a region producing or releasing
assimilates, such as a photosynthesising leaf. A sink is a region using or
storing assimilates, such as roots, fruits, seeds or growing tissues.

Translocation allows products of photosynthesis to reach parts of the plant that
cannot photosynthesise sufficiently. Unlike xylem transport, phloem transport
can occur in different directions depending on source and sink relationships.

subtopics.title: Plant Coordination and Response
subtopics.content:
Plants respond to environmental stimuli including light, gravity, water and
touch. Growth responses are called tropisms.

Phototropism is growth in response to light. Shoots generally show positive
phototropism and roots commonly show negative phototropism. Geotropism/
gravitropism describes growth in response to gravity; roots generally grow
positively while shoots grow negatively.

Auxin is a plant hormone involved in growth responses. In shoots, unequal auxin
distribution can cause cells on the shaded side to elongate more, bending the
shoot towards light.

subtopics.title: Plant Reproduction
subtopics.content:
Asexual reproduction produces offspring from a single parent without fusion of
gametes. It usually produces genetically similar offspring. Vegetative
propagation occurs through structures such as runners, bulbs, tubers and
cuttings.

Sexual reproduction involves fusion of male and female gametes. In flowering
plants, pollen grains contain the male gametes and the ovule contains the female
gamete. Pollination is transfer of pollen from anther to stigma. Fertilisation
occurs when the male gamete fuses with the egg cell.

After fertilisation the ovule develops into a seed and the ovary develops into
a fruit. Seeds contain an embryo and food reserves and can be dispersed and
germinated under suitable conditions.

subtopics.title: Human Nutrition and Balanced Diet
subtopics.content:
A balanced diet provides the nutrients and energy required for normal
metabolism, growth, repair and health. Major nutrient groups are carbohydrates,
proteins, fats, vitamins, mineral salts, fibre and water.

Carbohydrates are important energy sources. Proteins provide amino acids needed
for growth and tissue repair. Fats provide concentrated energy, insulation and
protection. Vitamins and mineral ions are required in smaller quantities for
specific functions. Fibre supports normal movement of food through the gut, and
water is essential for transport and metabolic reactions.

Energy requirements vary with age, sex, body size, activity level, growth,
pregnancy and environmental conditions. Malnutrition includes both deficiency
and excess. Deficiency diseases include scurvy from vitamin C deficiency,
rickets from inadequate vitamin D/calcium exposure, anaemia associated with
insufficient iron and protein-energy malnutrition.

subtopics.title: Digestive System and Digestion
subtopics.content:
Digestion converts large, insoluble food molecules into smaller soluble
molecules that can be absorbed.

Ingestion occurs at the mouth. Teeth mechanically break food into smaller pieces
and saliva moistens it. Salivary amylase begins starch digestion.

Food passes through the oesophagus by peristalsis. In the stomach, muscular
churning mixes food and gastric secretions; hydrochloric acid provides an acidic
environment and helps control microbes, while proteases begin protein digestion.

The small intestine receives bile and pancreatic juice. Bile neutralises acidic
chyme and emulsifies fats, increasing surface area for lipase. Pancreatic and
intestinal enzymes complete digestion. The large intestine absorbs water and
forms faeces, which leave through the rectum and anus.

subtopics.title: Absorption and Assimilation
subtopics.content:
The small intestine is adapted for absorption by its great length, folded
lining and numerous villi. Villi provide a large surface area. The epithelial
layer is thin, allowing a short diffusion distance. Each villus contains a
blood capillary network and a lacteal.

Glucose and amino acids enter blood capillaries. Products of fat digestion enter
the lacteals and are transported through the lymphatic system before reaching
the blood.

Assimilation is the incorporation and use of absorbed nutrients by cells. Glucose
may be used in respiration or stored as glycogen. Amino acids are used to make
proteins.

subtopics.title: Gaseous Exchange in Humans
subtopics.content:
The lungs provide a large, moist surface for gas exchange. Air travels through
the nose/mouth, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles and finally to alveoli.

Alveoli have a large total surface area, very thin walls, a moist lining and a
rich capillary supply. These features maintain a steep concentration gradient
and short diffusion distance for oxygen and carbon dioxide.

Ventilation continually replaces air in the alveoli. Oxygen diffuses into blood
and combines reversibly with haemoglobin in red blood cells. Carbon dioxide
diffuses from blood into alveoli and is exhaled.

subtopics.title: Transport: Blood, Heart and Circulation
subtopics.content:
Blood consists of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
Plasma transports dissolved nutrients, hormones, carbon dioxide, urea and heat.
Red blood cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin. White blood cells defend against
pathogens. Platelets help blood clot.

The heart is a muscular pump with four chambers: right and left atria and right
and left ventricles. Valves prevent backflow. The right side pumps
deoxygenated blood to the lungs; the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the
rest of the body.

Humans have double circulation. Pulmonary circulation carries blood between the
heart and lungs; systemic circulation carries blood between the heart and body.

Arteries carry blood away from the heart and have thick elastic walls. Veins
return blood to the heart and have valves. Capillaries have very thin walls for
exchange of substances with tissues.

subtopics.title: Homeostasis and the Kidney
subtopics.content:
Homeostasis is maintenance of a relatively stable internal environment despite
external or internal changes. Important variables include body temperature,
blood glucose concentration and water balance.

The kidneys remove urea and regulate water and mineral ion balance. Urea is
formed in the liver from excess amino acids and is transported in blood to the
kidneys.

In the nephron, blood is filtered at the glomerulus. Useful substances such as
glucose and much of the water and ions are selectively reabsorbed. The final
urine contains water, urea and excess ions.

Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) increases water reabsorption in the kidney collecting
ducts. When body water is low, more ADH is released, producing a smaller volume
of concentrated urine. When water is abundant, less ADH is released and urine
becomes more dilute.

subtopics.title: Coordination and Response
subtopics.content:
The nervous system detects stimuli, processes information and coordinates rapid
responses. Receptors detect changes in the environment. Sensory neurones carry
impulses towards the central nervous system; relay neurones occur mainly in the
central nervous system; motor neurones carry impulses to effectors.

A reflex action is a rapid, automatic response that helps protect the body.
A typical reflex arc involves receptor -> sensory neurone -> relay neurone ->
motor neurone -> effector.

Synapses are junctions between neurones. Neurotransmitters carry signals across
the synaptic gap. The one-way nature of synaptic transmission helps establish
direction in neural pathways.

subtopics.title: Endocrine System
subtopics.content:
Endocrine glands release hormones into the blood. Hormones are chemical
messengers that affect target cells possessing suitable receptors.

Insulin lowers blood glucose concentration by promoting uptake and storage of
glucose, including conversion to glycogen. Glucagon has an opposing role in
raising blood glucose when it falls.

Adrenaline prepares the body for rapid action by increasing heart rate and
increasing blood supply to muscles. Other hormones regulate growth,
reproduction, metabolism and water balance.

subtopics.title: Skeletal System and Movement
subtopics.content:
The skeleton supports the body, protects internal organs, provides attachment
points for muscles and enables movement. Joints occur where bones meet.

At a synovial joint, cartilage reduces friction and absorbs shock. Synovial
fluid lubricates the joint. Ligaments connect bone to bone and help stabilise
joints.

Skeletal muscles work by contraction. Muscles often operate as antagonistic
pairs: when one muscle contracts, the opposing muscle relaxes. At the elbow,
the biceps and triceps provide a common example.

subtopics.title: Human Reproduction
subtopics.content:
Sexual reproduction involves fusion of male and female gametes to form a
zygote. Puberty is the period when reproductive organs mature and secondary
sexual characteristics develop.

The male reproductive system includes testes, epididymis, sperm ducts, glands,
urethra, penis and scrotum. Testes produce sperm and testosterone. The scrotum
helps maintain a temperature suitable for sperm production.

The female reproductive system includes ovaries, oviducts, uterus, cervix and
vagina. Ovaries release ova and produce hormones such as oestrogen and
progesterone. Fertilisation normally occurs in the oviduct.

During pregnancy the embryo develops in the uterus. The placenta permits exchange
of oxygen, nutrients and wastes between maternal and fetal blood without direct
mixing of the two blood supplies. The umbilical cord connects the fetus to the
placenta.

Menstruation, ovulation and hormonal changes form part of the reproductive
cycle. Contraception can prevent fertilisation or implantation and is relevant
to family planning and reproductive health.

subtopics.title: Aerobic Respiration
subtopics.content:
Respiration is the series of chemical reactions in cells that releases usable
energy from food molecules. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen.

The word equation is:
glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy.

Energy released is captured largely in ATP, which powers active transport,
muscle contraction, synthesis of molecules, growth, repair and other cellular
work. Mitochondria are major sites of aerobic respiration.

The rate of respiration is affected by factors including temperature, oxygen
availability, substrate availability and activity of tissues.

subtopics.title: Anaerobic Respiration
subtopics.content:
Anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen and releases less energy from each
glucose molecule because breakdown is incomplete.

In human muscles, anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid. During vigorous
activity, oxygen supply may not meet demand. Lactic acid accumulation is
associated with fatigue and must subsequently be processed when oxygen becomes
available.

In yeast, anaerobic respiration produces ethanol and carbon dioxide. This
fermentation is useful in bread making and alcoholic beverage production.

subtopics.title: Energy Transfer and Exercise
subtopics.content:
During exercise, muscles require increased ATP. Heart rate and breathing rate
rise to increase oxygen and nutrient delivery and remove carbon dioxide.

If oxygen delivery is insufficient, anaerobic pathways contribute to ATP
production. Recovery requires continued oxygen uptake to restore normal
conditions and process accumulated metabolic products.

Respiration links nutrition, gaseous exchange and circulation: food supplies
respiratory substrates, lungs supply oxygen, blood transports materials and
cells release usable energy.

subtopics.title: Microorganisms
subtopics.content:
Microorganisms are organisms or biological entities too small to be seen clearly
without magnification. Important groups studied at this level include bacteria,
fungi, protozoa and microscopic algae; viruses are acellular infectious agents
rather than cellular organisms.

Microorganisms vary in structure and nutrition. Bacteria are prokaryotic cells
without a membrane-bound nucleus. Fungi such as yeast are eukaryotic. Many
microorganisms reproduce rapidly under suitable conditions.

Microorganisms can be beneficial or harmful. Beneficial microorganisms are used
in fermentation, decomposition, food production, biotechnology and nutrient
cycling. Harmful microorganisms can cause infectious diseases and food
spoilage.

subtopics.title: Economic Importance of Microorganisms
subtopics.content:
Yeast ferments sugars and produces carbon dioxide and ethanol. Carbon dioxide
makes bread dough rise. Bacteria are used in yoghurt and other fermented foods.

Microorganisms are decomposers and recycle nutrients. Industrial fermentation
can produce antibiotics, enzymes, organic acids, alcohol and other useful
substances.

In agriculture, microorganisms contribute to decomposition and nutrient
cycling. Some bacteria convert nitrogen into forms that can become available to
plants.

subtopics.title: Recombinant DNA Technology
subtopics.content:
Recombinant DNA technology combines DNA from different sources. A desired gene
can be isolated or copied and inserted into a suitable vector such as a
bacterial plasmid. The recombinant DNA is introduced into host cells where the
gene may be expressed.

A simplified sequence is: identify the desired gene -> obtain or amplify the
gene -> cut or prepare DNA and vector -> join the gene to the vector -> insert
recombinant DNA into host cells -> select suitable cells -> grow cells and
obtain the product.

Restriction enzymes recognise specific DNA sequences and cut DNA. DNA ligase
joins DNA fragments. Plasmids can act as vectors because they replicate in
bacteria and can carry inserted genes.

Recombinant DNA technology has applications in production of medicines such as
human insulin, vaccine development, agriculture and research. Ethical,
environmental and biosafety issues must also be considered.

subtopics.title: Insulin Production
subtopics.content:
Human insulin can be produced using genetically modified microorganisms. The
human insulin gene is introduced into a suitable host using recombinant DNA
methods. The host produces insulin, which can then be harvested and purified.

Large-scale production requires controlled growth conditions, sterile
equipment, monitoring of temperature and pH, separation of the product and
purification. Biotechnology can therefore make medicines available at scale.

subtopics.title: Microbial Growth and Control
subtopics.content:
Microorganisms grow rapidly when temperature, moisture, nutrients and pH are
suitable. Growth can be controlled by refrigeration, heating, drying, chemical
preservatives, antiseptics, disinfectants and appropriate sterilisation.

Aseptic technique reduces unwanted contamination. In school practical work,
cultures should be handled according to laboratory safety rules and should not
be opened unnecessarily.

subtopics.title: Chromosomes, Genes and DNA
subtopics.content:
A chromosome is a long DNA molecule associated with proteins. A gene is a section
of DNA that contains information influencing a particular characteristic,
commonly through coding for a functional RNA or protein.

Chromosomes occur in pairs in diploid body cells. A pair of corresponding
chromosomes is homologous. Different forms of a gene are called alleles.

During cell division, chromosomes are copied so genetic information can be passed
to daughter cells. Gametes contain one set of chromosomes, so fertilisation
restores the diploid number.

subtopics.title: Monohybrid Inheritance
subtopics.content:
A monohybrid cross follows inheritance of one characteristic. A dominant allele
is expressed in the phenotype when present in a heterozygote, while a recessive
allele is expressed when no dominant allele is present.

Genotype describes the allele combination, while phenotype describes the
observable characteristic. Homozygous means two identical alleles; heterozygous
means two different alleles.

For a cross between two heterozygotes, Aa x Aa, the possible offspring
genotypes are AA, Aa, Aa and aa, giving a theoretical 1:2:1 genotype ratio and
a 3:1 phenotype ratio where complete dominance applies.

Genetic crosses should use clearly defined allele symbols and distinguish
parental generation, gametes, offspring genotypes and phenotypes.

subtopics.title: ABO Blood Groups and Sex Determination
subtopics.content:
The ABO blood group system is an example of multiple alleles. The main alleles
are IA, IB and i. IA and IB are codominant with each other, while i is recessive.

Genotype IAIA or IAi gives blood group A; IBIB or IBi gives group B; IAIB gives
group AB; ii gives group O.

Human sex is associated with X and Y chromosomes. Females commonly have XX and
males commonly have XY. Eggs carry X, while sperm may carry X or Y. Therefore
the sperm determines whether the resulting embryo is XX or XY in the usual
chromosomal system.

subtopics.content:
A sex-linked gene is located on a sex chromosome. X-linked traits are often
discussed because males have only one X chromosome, so a recessive allele on
their X chromosome may be expressed.

Genetic diagrams for sex-linked inheritance should identify the chromosome and
allele, for example X^A and X^a. A carrier female may have one normal allele and
one recessive allele and may pass the allele to sons or daughters.

subtopics.content:
A mutation is a change in genetic material. Mutations may involve a change in a
gene sequence or a change in chromosome structure or number.

Mutations can arise spontaneously or from mutagens such as certain forms of
radiation and chemicals. Their effects range from negligible to harmful or,
less commonly, beneficial.

Chromosomal abnormalities can result from errors during cell division. Genetic
disorders can be inherited when altered alleles are transmitted from parents.

cell-cycle regulation.

subtopics.content:
Variation means differences between individuals of the same species. Genetic
variation can arise through mutation, recombination and the random distribution
of chromosomes and gametes.

Discontinuous variation produces distinct categories, such as ABO blood groups.
Continuous variation shows a range of values, such as height or mass, and is
commonly influenced by several genes and environmental factors.

subtopics.title: Natural and Artificial Selection
subtopics.content:
Natural selection occurs when individuals with advantageous heritable
characteristics survive and reproduce more successfully in a particular
environment. Their alleles can become more common over generations.

Selection requires variation, inheritance, competition and differential survival
or reproduction. Environmental changes can alter which characteristics are
advantageous.

Artificial selection is controlled by humans. Individuals with desired
characteristics are selected as parents and bred over generations. In
agriculture this can improve yield, disease resistance, growth rate or quality,
but excessive selection can reduce genetic diversity.

subtopics.title: Meaning and Importance of Biodiversity
subtopics.content:
Biodiversity is the variety of life at genetic, species and ecosystem levels.
It includes the diversity within species, between species and among ecosystems.

Biodiversity provides food, medicines, fibres, genetic resources, pollination,
soil formation, nutrient cycling, water regulation and cultural value. Healthy
ecosystems can be more resilient when they contain appropriate biological
diversity.

Zimbabwe has diverse habitats including forests, grasslands, wetlands,
freshwater systems and savanna ecosystems. Conservation decisions should
consider both biological value and sustainable community needs.

subtopics.title: Classification of Organisms
subtopics.content:
Classification groups organisms according to shared characteristics and
evolutionary relationships. Scientific names reduce confusion caused by local
names.

A traditional five-kingdom scheme recognises Monera, Protoctista, Fungi, Plantae
and Animalia. Modern classification may use domains and phylogenetic
relationships, but the five-kingdom framework remains useful for school-level
comparisons.

Plants are generally multicellular, photosynthetic eukaryotes with cellulose
cell walls. Animals are multicellular heterotrophs without cell walls. Fungi
have chitinous cell walls and obtain nutrients by absorption. Protists are a
diverse group of mainly unicellular or simple eukaryotes. Bacteria are
prokaryotic organisms.

subtopics.title: Threats to Biodiversity
subtopics.content:
Major threats include habitat destruction, habitat fragmentation, pollution,
overexploitation, invasive species, climate change, disease and illegal
wildlife trade.

Habitat destruction removes resources required for feeding, breeding and
shelter. Fragmentation can isolate populations and reduce gene flow.
Overharvesting can reduce populations faster than they reproduce. Pollution can
alter water, soil and air quality.

Climate change can alter temperature, rainfall and seasonal patterns, forcing
species to move or adapt. Species unable to cope may decline.

subtopics.title: Conservation Measures
subtopics.content:
In-situ conservation protects organisms within their natural habitats. Examples
include national parks, wildlife areas, forest reserves and protected wetlands.

Ex-situ conservation protects organisms outside their natural habitats, such as
botanical gardens, seed banks, zoos and captive breeding programmes.

Other measures include sustainable harvesting, anti-poaching enforcement,
habitat restoration, environmental education, community participation,
pollution control and responsible land management.

subtopics.title: Components of Ecosystems
subtopics.content:
An ecosystem consists of living organisms and the non-living environment with
which they interact. Biotic components include producers, consumers and
decomposers. Abiotic factors include light intensity, temperature, rainfall,
soil pH, mineral availability, water availability and wind.

organisms of the same species living in an area. A community consists of
populations of different species interacting in an area.

subtopics.title: Food Chains, Food Webs and Trophic Levels
subtopics.content:
A food chain shows a feeding sequence. It normally begins with a producer,
followed by consumers. Arrows represent the direction of energy transfer.

Food webs show interconnected feeding relationships. A trophic level is a
position in a food chain, such as producer, primary consumer, secondary
consumer and higher consumers.

Energy enters most ecosystems through sunlight captured by producers. Energy is
lost at each trophic transfer through respiration, movement, heat and waste.

A pyramid of biomass represents the total dry mass of organisms at each level.

subtopics.content:
Carbon dioxide is removed from the atmosphere by photosynthesis and incorporated
into organic molecules. Carbon passes through food chains when organisms feed.

Respiration returns carbon dioxide to the atmosphere. Decomposition returns
carbon compounds to soil and releases carbon dioxide. Combustion of wood and
fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide. Carbon can also be stored in biomass,
soils, sediments and fossil fuels.

Human activities such as deforestation and burning fossil fuels can increase
atmospheric carbon dioxide and influence climate change.

Nitrogen is essential for amino acids, proteins and nucleic acids. Atmospheric
nitrogen gas cannot be used directly by most plants.

Nitrogen-fixing microorganisms convert nitrogen gas into usable nitrogen
compounds. Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia/ammonium compounds through
nitrite to nitrate. Plants absorb nitrate ions and incorporate nitrogen into
organic compounds.

Animals obtain nitrogen by feeding. Decomposers break down nitrogen-containing
waste and dead organisms. Denitrifying bacteria return nitrogen gas to the
atmosphere.

Excess fertiliser can enter waterways and promote eutrophication.

subtopics.title: Population and Community Interactions
subtopics.content:
Populations change through births, deaths, immigration and emigration. Carrying
capacity is the population size an environment can support over time.

Organisms compete for resources such as food, water, light, space and mates.
Predation affects population sizes and can produce cycles between predator and
prey populations.

commensalism. The outcome depends on the species and environmental conditions.

subtopics.title: Ecosystem Management
subtopics.content:
Ecosystem management aims to maintain productivity, biodiversity and ecological
stability while allowing sustainable use of resources.

Natural systems include forests, grasslands, rivers, wetlands and savannas.
Artificial systems include crop fields, plantations, dams, gardens and managed
livestock systems.

Sustainable management can include controlled grazing, crop rotation,
conservation agriculture, reforestation, wetland protection, soil conservation,
water management and appropriate use of fire.

Good management monitors environmental indicators, recognises local knowledge,
reduces waste and considers long-term consequences.

subtopics.title: Health and Factors Affecting Health
subtopics.content:
Health is a state of physical, mental and social well-being rather than merely
the absence of disease.

Health is influenced by nutrition, sanitation, clean water, housing, exercise,
rest, personal hygiene, access to healthcare, environmental conditions,
behaviour and social circumstances.

subtopics.title: Infectious and Non-Infectious Diseases
subtopics.content:
Infectious diseases are caused by pathogens and can be transmitted directly or
indirectly. Pathogens include bacteria, viruses, fungi and protozoa.

Non-infectious diseases are not normally transmitted between people. They may
result from genetic factors, nutritional deficiencies, lifestyle, environmental
exposure or abnormal cell growth.

Prevention depends on the cause. Infectious diseases may be controlled through
hygiene, sanitation, vaccination, isolation, vector control and appropriate
treatment. Non-infectious disease risk may be reduced by balanced nutrition,
physical activity, avoiding tobacco and harmful drug use, and regular medical
care.

subtopics.title: Transmission of Pathogens
subtopics.content:
Pathogens may spread through droplets, direct contact, contaminated food and
water, blood, sexual contact, contaminated objects or vectors such as mosquitoes.

Breaking the chain of transmission involves identifying the route and
interrupting it. Examples include handwashing, safe food preparation, clean
water, proper waste disposal, mosquito control, safe handling of blood and
vaccination.

immune response.

subtopics.title: Selected Diseases Relevant to Zimbabwe
subtopics.content:
Malaria is transmitted by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. Prevention
includes reducing mosquito exposure, using insecticide-treated nets and
appropriate vector-control measures.

Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious disease that commonly affects the lungs and
spreads through airborne droplets from infected people. Persistent cough,
weight loss, fever and night sweats can occur. Diagnosis and completion of
prescribed treatment are important for control.

Cholera is associated with contaminated water or food and can cause severe
diarrhoea and dehydration. Safe water, sanitation, hygiene and prompt treatment
help prevent deaths and transmission.

HIV attacks cells involved in immune defence and can lead to AIDS if untreated.
HIV can be transmitted through infected blood, sexual transmission and from
mother to child. It is not spread by ordinary casual contact such as shaking
hands. Prevention includes informed safer-sex practices, sterile equipment,
testing, treatment and prevention of mother-to-child transmission.

Disease discussions should distinguish scientifically established transmission
routes from myths and stigma.

subtopics.title: Immunity, Vaccination and Antibodies
subtopics.content:
The immune system protects the body against pathogens. White blood cells can
engulf pathogens and some lymphocytes produce antibodies.

An antibody is a protein that binds specifically to an antigen. Specific
antibodies help identify and neutralise pathogens or mark them for destruction.

Active immunity develops when the body's immune system produces its own
antibodies and memory cells after infection or vaccination. Passive immunity
results from receiving antibodies from another source and is usually temporary.

Vaccination exposes the immune system to harmless forms or components associated
with a pathogen so that memory cells develop without causing the full disease.
Later exposure can trigger a faster and stronger response.

subtopics.title: Drug Use and Abuse
subtopics.content:
Medicines are substances used to prevent, diagnose or treat disease. Correct
dosage, route and duration are important. Antibiotics act against susceptible
bacteria and do not cure viral infections.

Drug abuse involves harmful or inappropriate use of substances. Possible
consequences include dependence, impaired judgement, organ damage, accidents,
social problems and overdose.

Antibiotic misuse can select resistant bacteria. Completing prescribed courses
and using antibiotics only when appropriately prescribed helps reduce
antimicrobial resistance.

subtopics.title: Cancer and Lifestyle-Related Disease
subtopics.content:
Cancer involves uncontrolled growth and division of abnormal cells. Some cancers
are associated with inherited mutations, while others are influenced by
environmental or lifestyle factors.

Risk factors can include tobacco smoke, excessive alcohol use, certain
infections, radiation and some occupational or environmental exposures.

Prevention and early detection can reduce disease burden. Screening programmes,
prompt medical assessment of warning signs and evidence-based treatment are
important components of cancer control.

use them in biological context, and distinguish closely related terms. In an
examination, definitions should identify the process, the direction or relationship
involved, and any condition that makes the definition precise.

Understanding relationships:
Biology questions often test relationships rather than isolated facts. When explaining
a process, state the starting condition, describe what changes, identify the mechanism
responsible, and state the result. Where a structure is described, link each important
feature to its function. Where a factor affects a process, state the direction of the
effect and explain the biological reason.

Application:
The knowledge in Cancer and Lifestyle-Related Disease should be applied to unfamiliar examples, diagrams, tables,
graphs and everyday situations. Students should practise identifying variables,
predicting outcomes, explaining observations and drawing conclusions supported by
evidence. Zimbabwean examples should be interpreted scientifically: local crops,
livestock, wildlife, water resources, public-health programmes and environmental
conditions can provide useful contexts for applying the same biological principles.

Practical skills:
For investigations related to this subtopic, identify the independent variable,
dependent variable and controlled variables. Use an appropriate control where
possible. Keep quantities and procedures consistent, repeat measurements, calculate
averages where appropriate, identify anomalous results, present results in a suitable
table or graph and draw a conclusion that directly answers the investigation question.
Safety precautions must be specific to the actual hazard rather than simply stating
"be careful".

Exam technique:
For a "state" question, give the required fact without unnecessary explanation. For
"describe", give observable features or sequential events. For "explain", give the
reason or mechanism. For "compare", provide paired similarities or differences using
the same basis of comparison. For "suggest", apply known biological principles to the
new situation and make the reasoning explicit. For calculations, show working,
include units and check whether the final value is biologically sensible.

Common errors to avoid:
Do not confuse structure with function, diffusion with osmosis, active transport with
passive transport, genotype with phenotype, or respiration with breathing. Do not use
arrows ambiguously in food chains. Do not claim that every change in phenotype is
caused by a change in DNA. Do not describe a correlation as proof of causation without
evidence. Use correct biological vocabulary and avoid everyday meanings where they
conflict with scientific meanings.

Revision checklist:
Before moving on, a learner should be able to define the central terms, explain the
main mechanism, label or interpret relevant biological structures, compare related
concepts, describe a suitable practical investigation, interpret simple experimental
data, and apply the topic to a new biological situation.
